title: South Carolina Mustard BBQ Sauce
subtitle: Yellow mustard and honey sauce from the South Carolina tradition
excerpt: South Carolina mustard sauce is a sharp, bright yellow condiment built on yellow mustard, cider vinegar, and honey. It's the defining sauce of the South Carolina barbecue belt and a genuine alternative to tomato-based sauces: lighter, sharper, and more tangy.
sourceNotes: South Carolina mustard-based barbecue sauce is a recognised regional tradition, particularly dominant in the central part of the state. The German immigrant community is credited with introducing mustard to the local barbecue tradition in the 18th and 19th centuries.

recipe.batchNotes: Make in larger quantities and keep refrigerated for up to three weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for three weeks in a sealed jar. The flavour mellows and improves after a day.

content.text: South Carolina mustard sauce is yellow, tangy, and sweet in a way that's entirely different from the thick tomato sauces of Kansas City. Made from yellow mustard, cider vinegar, honey, and a little brown sugar, it takes ten minutes and clings well to pulled pork and grilled sausages. The mustard gives it a warmth that intensifies as the sauce cooks down.
Combine all the ingredients in a small saucepan and stir until mixed.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring, for eight to ten minutes until the sugar dissolves and the sauce thickens slightly. If using {{unsalted-butter}}, stir it in off the heat for a glossier finish.
Taste and adjust: more honey for sweetness, more vinegar for sharpness, more cayenne for heat. The sauce should be a balance of tangy and sweet with a clean mustard warmth.

items.symptom: The sauce is too sharp and acidic
items.cause: Cider vinegar sharpness varies by brand.
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of honey and stir well. The sweetness should round the vinegar without masking the mustard character.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thick and stiff
items.cause: Reduced too much, or the honey caramelised too quickly.
items.fix: Add a splash of water or more cider vinegar and stir over low heat to loosen. The sauce thickens as it cools.

items.symptom: The mustard flavour is too harsh
items.cause: English mustard is sharper than American yellow mustard.
items.fix: Use half English and half Dijon, or reduce the amount of mustard slightly. The harshness mellows as the sauce cooks.

items.symptom: The sauce looks separated and grainy
items.cause: Heat too high and the sugar crystallised.
items.fix: Take off the heat, add a tablespoon of water, and stir vigorously. If using butter, it will help re-emulsify the sauce.

content.text: Mustard sauce is the signature of the South Carolina barbecue belt. This zone runs through the middle of the state, distinct from Kansas City tomato sauces and eastern Carolina vinegar sauces. German settlers in the 18th century are thought to have introduced mustard with pork, which evolved into this yellow sauce. Use it on pulled pork, bratwurst, or as a dipping sauce for chicken.
